title: MB9-08953
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
For the following reasons, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) allows the appeal and refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.

In her Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant alleges a fear of criminals in Mexico who are possibly linked to the government and who allegedly want to hurt her due to the activities of her father, who runs XXXX and XXXX that denounce state corruption. The appellant was allegedly the subject of an attempted kidnapping on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, the appellant left Mexico for Canada, where she claimed refugee protection.
Following a hearing on March 26, 2019, and in written reasons dated April 12, 2019, the RPD rejected the refugee protection claim on the ground that the appellant's allegations were not credible.

The appellant submits before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) that the RPD erred in its assessment of her credibility for reasons that will be discussed below in the Analysis section, if necessary. STANDARD OF REVIEW AND THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION'S ROLE

The RAD's role is to review RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard of review after carrying out its own analysis of the record to determine whether the RPD erred, as submitted by the appellant. The exception to this rule concerns the RPD's findings in the assessment of credibility or the weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears. In situations where it enjoyed a meaningful advantage, the RAD must then show a degree of deference to the RPD's findings (Canada v. Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93, No. A-470-14). If I am of the opinion that the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage, I will provide reasons in my analysis.

The appellant filed before the RAD two documents that she claims constitute new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), which states that: On appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

In addition to the explicit conditions set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the RAD must also consider the implicit conditions pertaining to the admissibility of new evidence, as established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Singh (M.C.I. v. Parminder Singh, 2016 FCA 96), and in particular, in this case, the criteria of credibility and relevance of new evidence.
The first document is titled Menace à ma vie [Threat to my life], is not dated and describes facts that allegedly occurred on July 28, 2015.
The second document is titled Demande au gouverneur du Mexique [Request to the Governor of Mexico] and is dated April 2008.

Both documents pre-date the date on which the claim was rejected, and the appellant does not explain why they were not available at that time or, if they were, why they were not reasonably presented at that time.
For this reason, I do not accept them as evidence before the RAD.
In addition, I note from reading these documents that I do not see how they would be relevant to the appellant's refugee protection claim.
In July 2020, the appellant sent the RAD what she believed was new evidence.

The first document appears to be a form from the National Institute of Copyright in Mexico that mentions the name of the appellant's father. This document is not dated. The second document appears to be a response from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to the appellant's father and is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2001. The date of the second document suggests that the first document also pre-dates the rejection of the claim.

The appellant does not explain why they were not available at that time or, if they were, why they were not reasonably presented at that time. Moreover, the appellant does not explain how these documents are relevant to her claim. For these reasons, I cannot accept them as evidence before the RAD.

The third document is a series of photographs that appear to be taken from a Google search. There is no explanation for the content or relevance of this document. For these reasons, I do not accept it as evidence before the RAD.

In any event, because I am referring the matter to the RPD, the appellant will be able to submit them if she wishes to do so, and the RPD accept them into evidence if they meet the requirements in this regard.
The issue in this case is whether the RPD erred in its analysis of the appellant's credibility.

After analyzing all the evidence presented, including listening to the recording of the hearing before the RPD, and taking into consideration its reasons and the appellant's submissions, respectfully, I am of the opinion that the answer to that question is yes.

The RPD's short decision is based on three elements raised, namely, the fact that the appellant testified in a [translation] "confusing manner" about her fear; the fact that her brothers and sisters in Mexico were apparently not targeted by the criminals; and a contradiction as to whether she went to the police alone or with her father following the alleged attempted kidnapping.

Considering the appellant's allegations as outlined in her BOC Form and her testimony before the RPD, I am of the opinion that the elements raised by the RPD are insufficient to reject the credibility of her allegations.
It is true that the appellant's testimony was quite difficult. The appellant testified with reluctance and sometimes even with some contradictions.
However, in my opinion, the appellant was not sufficiently questioned about the allegations in her BOC Form and did not have the opportunity to explain possible contradictions and implausibilities.

For example, the appellant was not asked any questions about her allegations that she was been confined and raped by a criminal group in 2009; when asked as to whether she had had [translation] "problems other" than those of XXXX 2017, she first answered "yes" before changing her answer to "no"; she states in her BOC Form that she was involved in her father's activities but testified that not really knowing what he does; she testified that she moved in with her father in XXXX 2017 to pursue her studies, which contradicts the answers to questions 7 (education) and 12 (addresses) of form IMM5669, which she completed as part of her refugee protection claim; the answers to questions 8 (personal history) and 9 (membership of association with organizations) of the same form also appear to contradict her allegations; no questions were asked about the absence of documents, primarily from her father and his organizations, that could corroborate the appellant's allegations.

I find that I am unable to determine whether the appellant's central allegations are credible, and the RAD cannot hold a hearing to question her, since no new evidence was admitted on appeal. I am also of the view that the issue of whether the appellant has an internal flight alternative in Mexico may be relevant in this case.
For this reason, I set aside the RPD's determination and refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.

I conclude that the RPD's decision is wrong in fact and in law, and I find that I am unable to properly assess the appellant's credibility and, if necessary, the issue of whether the appellant has an internal flight alternative, without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD.

The appeal is allowed.
